questions.questionText: What is the difference between StatelessWidget and StatefulWidget?

options.text: StatelessWidget holds mutable state; StatefulWidget does not.
StatelessWidget describes a widget that never changes; StatefulWidget can rebuild when its state changes.
StatelessWidget is faster because it always uses const constructors.
There is no functional difference — it's purely stylistic.

questions.explanation: A StatelessWidget describes a part of the user interface that can only depend on its configuration and the BuildContext. A StatefulWidget, on the other hand, creates a State object that can hold mutable data and trigger rebuilds via setState().

questions.questionText: Which widget should you use to create a scrollable list of children that are built lazily?

options.text: Column
ListView
Stack
Row

questions.explanation: ListView builds its children lazily, meaning only the items visible on screen (plus a small buffer) are built and rendered. Column, by contrast, builds all children at once and does not scroll by default.

questions.questionText: Which of the following are valid layout widgets in Flutter? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Row
Column
Stack
Navigator

questions.explanation: Row, Column, and Stack are all layout widgets. Row and Column place children linearly (horizontal and vertical respectively). Stack overlaps children. Navigator is a routing widget, not a layout widget.

questions.questionText: What does the `const` keyword do when applied to a widget constructor?

options.text: It prevents the widget from ever being garbage collected.
It marks the widget as compile-time constant, allowing Flutter to reuse the same instance and skip rebuilds.
It makes the widget read-only at runtime.
It has no practical effect — it's a style convention.

questions.explanation: Using `const` for a widget constructor creates a compile-time constant. Flutter can identify that two `const` widgets with the same arguments are identical and reuse the existing element tree, skipping expensive rebuilds.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the `BuildContext` passed to a widget's `build` method?

options.text: It is a handle to the widget's location in the widget tree.
It stores the widget's internal state.
It is used to configure HTTP requests.
It represents the platform (Android or iOS).

questions.explanation: BuildContext is a reference to the location of a widget within the widget tree. It is used by Flutter to traverse up the tree to find inherited widgets (e.g., Theme, MediaQuery, Navigator) and to access the surrounding context.

questions.questionText: What Flutter widget class would you extend to create a widget that never needs to rebuild based on external state changes?
questions.explanation: StatelessWidget is the base class for widgets that have no mutable state. Its `build` method is called only when the parent rebuilds it or when its own configuration (constructor arguments) changes.

questions.questionText: Which method in a StatefulWidget's State class is called exactly once when the State object is first inserted into the tree?

options.text: build()
didUpdateWidget()
initState()
dispose()

questions.explanation: initState() is called once when the State object is created and inserted into the tree. It is the correct place to do one-time setup such as subscribing to streams or initializing controllers.

questions.questionText: Which lifecycle methods should you override to clean up resources in a StatefulWidget? (Select all that apply)

options.text: dispose()
deactivate()
initState()
build()

questions.explanation: dispose() is the primary place to release resources (cancel timers, close streams, dispose controllers). deactivate() is called when the State is removed from the tree temporarily and can also be used for cleanup.

questions.questionText: In Dart null safety, what does the `?` suffix on a type (e.g., `String?`) mean?

options.text: The variable is optional and can be omitted from function calls.
The variable may hold either a value of that type or null.
The variable uses lazy evaluation.
The variable can only be set once.

questions.explanation: In Dart's sound null safety system, `String?` means the variable is *nullable* — it can hold a String value or null. Without the `?`, the type is non-nullable and the compiler guarantees it will never be null.

options.text: null
A compile error

questions.explanation: The `??` operator (null-coalescing operator) returns the left-hand operand if it is non-null, otherwise returns the right-hand operand. Since `x` is null, the expression evaluates to 42.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the `async` and `await` keywords in Dart?

options.text: They enable multi-threaded parallel execution.
They allow writing asynchronous code in a sequential, readable style using Futures.
They are used exclusively for network requests.
They prevent any code from running until the awaited task completes.

questions.explanation: Dart is single-threaded. The `async`/`await` syntax is syntactic sugar over Futures — it allows you to write async code that looks sequential and readable without callbacks. The event loop continues to process other events while awaiting.

questions.questionText: Which of the following are valid ways to declare a constant in Dart? (Select all that apply)

options.text: const int x = 5;
final int x = 5;
static int x = 5;
readonly int x = 5;

questions.explanation: `const` declares a compile-time constant (the value must be known at compile time). `final` declares a run-time constant (assigned once, cannot be reassigned). `static` is not a constant modifier; `readonly` is not valid Dart syntax.

questions.questionText: What does the `late` keyword do in Dart?

options.text: It marks a variable as deprecated.
It declares a non-nullable variable that will be initialized before its first use.
It enables lazy loading of packages.
It creates a variable that can only be accessed after a delay.

questions.explanation: The `late` modifier tells the Dart compiler 'I will initialize this non-nullable variable before it is ever read'. If you read a `late` variable before it is initialized, a LateInitializationError is thrown at runtime.

questions.questionText: What keyword do you use in Dart to define a function that returns a Stream of values over time?
questions.explanation: An `async*` function (async generator) uses `yield` to emit values to a Stream. Each `yield` statement pushes a new value to the stream without terminating the function.

questions.questionText: In Dart, which collection literal creates an immutable, ordered set of unique values?

options.text: const {...}

questions.explanation: `const {...}` creates a compile-time constant, immutable Set. Without `const`, `{...}` creates a mutable LinkedHashSet. `[...]` creates a List, not a Set.

questions.questionText: What is the cascade operator `..` used for in Dart?

options.text: It chains null-safe method calls.
It performs multiple operations on the same object without repeating the variable name.
It spreads the contents of one list into another.
It is used to inherit from multiple classes.

questions.explanation: The cascade operator `..` allows you to make a sequence of operations on the same object. For example: `paint..color = Colors.red..strokeWidth = 5` sets two properties on the same Paint object without repeating `paint.`.

questions.questionText: In Riverpod, which provider type is best suited for managing a list that can be modified (e.g., a to-do list)?

options.text: Provider
FutureProvider
StateNotifierProvider
StreamProvider

questions.explanation: StateNotifierProvider exposes a StateNotifier which holds immutable state and provides methods to mutate it. It is ideal for complex, mutable state objects like lists. Provider is read-only, FutureProvider is for async data, and StreamProvider is for streams.

questions.questionText: What does `ref.watch()` do in Riverpod, and how does it differ from `ref.read()`?

options.text: `ref.watch()` rebuilds the widget when the provider changes; `ref.read()` reads the value once without subscribing.
`ref.watch()` is for async providers; `ref.read()` is for sync providers.
They are identical — both subscribe to the provider.
`ref.read()` is preferred in build methods; `ref.watch()` is for event handlers.

questions.explanation: `ref.watch()` creates a subscription: when the watched provider's value changes, the widget rebuilds. `ref.read()` reads the current value without subscribing — it is safe to use inside callbacks/event handlers where rebuilds are not desired.

questions.questionText: Which of the following are advantages of using Riverpod for state management? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Providers are compile-time safe and testable outside the widget tree.
It uses BuildContext to locate providers, making it explicit.
Providers can depend on other providers forming a dependency graph.
It supports auto-dispose to free resources when providers are no longer listened to.

questions.explanation: Riverpod providers are declared globally and are compile-time safe. They can form dependency graphs (one provider watching another). Auto-dispose frees resources automatically. Unlike Provider, Riverpod does NOT require BuildContext to read a provider.

questions.questionText: In the BLoC pattern, what is the role of an 'Event'?

options.text: It represents the current UI state to be rendered.
It is an input dispatched to the BLoC representing something that happened.
It is a callback that runs after a state transition.
It is a type of widget that reacts to state changes.

questions.explanation: In BLoC, Events are inputs — they represent things that happen (user tapped a button, data loaded, etc.). The BLoC processes events and emits new States. The UI listens to States and dispatches Events.

questions.questionText: What is the main difference between `setState()` and a state management solution like Riverpod?

options.text: `setState()` requires more boilerplate than Riverpod.
`setState()` is local to a widget subtree; Riverpod provides global, shared state accessible from anywhere.
Riverpod is always faster than `setState()`.
`setState()` is deprecated and should not be used.

questions.explanation: `setState()` triggers a rebuild of only the calling State and its subtree — it is inherently local. Riverpod providers exist outside the widget tree and can be read or watched by any widget anywhere in the app, making them suitable for shared or app-wide state.

questions.questionText: In Riverpod, what class do you extend to create a notifier that manages complex state with multiple update methods?
questions.explanation: StateNotifier<T> is the base class for notifiers in Riverpod. It holds an immutable state T and exposes it via the `state` getter. Subclasses define methods that update `state`, triggering rebuilds in all watchers.

questions.questionText: Why is it important to use immutable state objects with StateNotifier?

options.text: Immutable objects are smaller in memory.
Riverpod uses value equality to detect state changes; mutating state in place bypasses change detection.
Dart requires all objects passed to StateNotifier to be immutable.
It's only a convention — mutable state works equally well.

questions.explanation: StateNotifier notifies listeners when `state` is replaced (not mutated). If you mutate the state object in place and re-assign the same reference, Riverpod sees no change and skips notifications. Always create a new object (e.g., via `copyWith()`) to replace state.

questions.questionText: In Flutter's Navigator, what does `push()` do?

options.text: It removes the current route from the navigation stack.
It adds a new route on top of the navigation stack.
It replaces the entire navigation stack with a new route.
It sends data to the previous route.

questions.explanation: Navigator.push() overlays a new route on top of the current stack. The back button or Navigator.pop() will remove it and return to the previous route.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between `Navigator.push()` and `Navigator.pushReplacement()`?

options.text: `pushReplacement()` adds the new route above the current route; `push()` replaces the entire stack.
`push()` adds the new route and keeps the current one; `pushReplacement()` removes the current route and adds the new one in its place.
They are identical.
`pushReplacement()` only works with named routes.

questions.explanation: `push()` adds the new route on top of the stack, leaving the current route visible behind it. `pushReplacement()` removes the current route and replaces it with the new one — useful for login → home transitions where you don't want back to return to login.

questions.questionText: Which of the following are advantages of GoRouter over Navigator 1.0? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Declarative route configuration using a list of GoRoute objects.
Built-in support for deep linking and URL-based navigation.
Redirect guards that can evaluate state before navigation.
It automatically generates navigation animations.

questions.explanation: GoRouter is a declarative router that maps URL paths to screens, supports deep links, and provides redirect guards (e.g., for authentication). It does not automatically generate custom animations — those must still be configured manually.

questions.questionText: In GoRouter, what is a `ShellRoute` used for?

options.text: It creates a shell/container (e.g., a bottom navigation bar) that persists across its child routes.
It is used to run native platform code from within Flutter.
It creates a modal overlay over the current route.
It defines a route that can only be accessed by authenticated users.

questions.explanation: ShellRoute wraps a set of child routes with a shared UI shell — commonly a Scaffold with a BottomNavigationBar. As the user navigates between the child routes, the shell widget stays on screen without rebuilding.

questions.questionText: How do you pass data from one route to another using GoRouter?

options.text: Only through URL path parameters (e.g., `/user/:id`).
Through URL path parameters, query parameters, or the `extra` argument on `context.go()`/`context.push()`.
Through a shared global variable.
GoRouter does not support passing data between routes.

questions.explanation: GoRouter supports multiple data passing mechanisms: path parameters (`:id` in routes), query parameters (`?key=value`), and an arbitrary `extra` object passed to `context.go()` or `context.push()`. The `extra` approach is most flexible but is not preserved across app restarts.

questions.questionText: What GoRouter method replaces the current route without leaving it on the navigation stack (equivalent to Navigator.pushReplacement)?
questions.explanation: `context.pushReplacement(path)` in GoRouter replaces the current top-most location on the stack. The previous route is removed so the user cannot navigate back to it with the back button.

questions.questionText: What happens when `context.go()` is called in GoRouter?

options.text: It pushes the new location on top of the current stack.
It navigates to the new location and clears the entire navigation stack, making it the new base.
It pops the current route and returns to the previous one.
It shows a dialog overlay at the new route.

questions.explanation: `context.go()` performs an absolute navigation — it replaces the entire navigation stack with the new location. Use `context.push()` when you want to add to the stack and allow the user to go back.
